questions.question: What is the SI unit of pressure?
questions.explanation: Pressure is measured in pascals (Pa), defined as one newton per square meter.
questions.fastStrategy: Pressure unit: Pa (N/m²).

questions.question: A barometer measures:
questions.explanation: Barometers measure atmospheric pressure. Thermometers measure temperature; anemometers measure wind speed; hygrometers measure humidity.
questions.fastStrategy: Barometer = air pressure meter.

questions.question: How does pressure change with depth in water?
questions.explanation: Pressure increases with depth because of the weight of the water above (P = ρgh).
questions.fastStrategy: Deeper in water → higher pressure.

questions.question: What happens to the buoyant force if an object displaces more fluid?
questions.explanation: Buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid. More displaced volume → greater buoyant force.
steps: Recall Archimedes: buoyant = weight of displaced fluid
More volume displaced → more fluid weight
questions.fastStrategy: Displace more fluid → buoyant force grows.

questions.question: Atmospheric pressure at high altitude is:
questions.explanation: With less air above, the weight of the air column decreases, so atmospheric pressure is lower.
steps: Pressure comes from air column weight
questions.fastStrategy: Higher up = lower air pressure.

questions.question: Which statement about gauge pressure in a car tire is correct?
questions.explanation: Gauge pressure is the pressure above atmospheric pressure. Absolute pressure = gauge + atmospheric.
questions.fastStrategy: Gauge pressure omits atmosphere; add atm to get absolute.

questions.question: If fluid density is halved, pressure at a given depth becomes:
questions.explanation: Pressure P = ρgh. Halving density halves the pressure at the same depth.
questions.fastStrategy: Lower density → lower pressure at same depth.

questions.question: Which fluid property resists flow?
questions.explanation: Viscosity measures resistance to flow. Density is mass/volume; surface tension relates to liquid surfaces.
steps: Surface tension is a surface effect
questions.fastStrategy: Flow resistance → viscosity.

questions.question: Hydraulic systems multiply force because:
questions.explanation: Equal pressure transmission means a small force on a small piston can create a larger force on a larger piston (Pascal's principle).
questions.fastStrategy: Equal pressure × larger area = larger force.

questions.question: The upward force on a wing (lift) is partly explained by:
questions.explanation: Bernoulli's principle relates faster airflow over the wing to lower pressure, contributing to lift.
questions.fastStrategy: Faster airflow → lower pressure → lift (Bernoulli contribution).

questions.question: Surface tension causes water to form:
questions.explanation: Surface tension pulls the surface to minimize area, forming nearly spherical droplets.
steps: Sphere has minimal area for volume
questions.fastStrategy: Surface tension → spherical droplets.

questions.question: Which factor increases pressure at the bottom of a container?
questions.explanation: Pressure from fluid weight depends on depth (P = ρgh). More depth increases pressure; container width doesn't matter.
questions.fastStrategy: Deeper fluid → higher bottom pressure.

questions.question: Which statement about fluid pressure is true?

choices.B: It acts equally in all directions
choices.D: It only acts at the surface

questions.explanation: In a static fluid, pressure at a point is isotropic—equal in all directions.
questions.fastStrategy: Static fluid pressure is directionless (same all ways).

questions.question: If atmospheric pressure is 101 kPa and a tire gauge reads 220 kPa, the tire's absolute pressure is:
questions.explanation: Gauge pressure is above atmospheric. Absolute pressure = 220 kPa (gauge) + 101 kPa (atmospheric) = 321 kPa.
questions.fastStrategy: Absolute = gauge + atmospheric.

questions.question: Why do your ears pop when ascending quickly?
questions.explanation: Outside pressure drops with altitude. Your middle ear adjusts to equalize pressure across the eardrum, causing a popping sensation.
questions.fastStrategy: Climbing lowers air pressure; ears equalize.

questions.question: What happens to air pressure inside a sealed bottle taken up a mountain?
questions.explanation: Inside a sealed bottle, the trapped air keeps the same pressure it had when sealed (neglecting temperature changes). Outside pressure drops, so the bottle may bulge.
steps: Without exchange, internal pressure stays near original
questions.fastStrategy: Sealed air keeps its initial pressure as you ascend (temp aside).

questions.question: Where is pressure greatest on a dam wall?
questions.explanation: Water pressure increases with depth, so the bottom experiences the highest pressure, requiring thicker walls there.
questions.fastStrategy: Deeper water pushes harder—bottom of dam gets most pressure.

questions.question: Which quantity is conserved in steady, incompressible flow (continuity equation)?
questions.explanation: Continuity states A1v1 = A2v2 for incompressible flow, meaning volume flow rate is constant along the pipe.
steps: Pressure can vary, velocity can change with area
questions.fastStrategy: Incompressible steady flow: A×v stays constant.

questions.question: Surface tension is stronger in water due to:
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules create relatively strong surface tension compared to many liquids.
steps: Identify cause of high surface tension
questions.fastStrategy: Water's surface tension comes from hydrogen bonds.

questions.question: If a small air bubble rises in water, the pressure inside the bubble as it rises will:
questions.explanation: As the bubble rises, external water pressure decreases, so the internal pressure drops and the bubble expands.
steps: Internal pressure adjusts lower, bubble expands
questions.fastStrategy: Rise → external pressure drops → bubble expands, internal pressure drops.

questions.question: What happens to the buoyant force on a fully submerged object if it is moved deeper (same fluid)?
questions.explanation: Buoyant force depends on displaced volume and fluid density, not depth (for incompressible fluids). Fully submerged volume is unchanged, so buoyant force stays the same.
steps: Buoyant force = weight of displaced volume
Volume and density unchanged with depth (incompressible)
questions.fastStrategy: Fully submerged: buoyant force doesn't change with depth (incompressible fluid).

questions.question: If oil (density < water) is poured on water, it floats because:

choices.B: Oil is less dense than water

questions.explanation: Less dense fluids float atop denser ones. Oil's density is lower than water's, so it floats.
steps: Lower density fluid sits above higher density fluid
questions.fastStrategy: Lower-density oil stays on top of water.

questions.question: The SI unit of density is:
questions.explanation: Density is mass per volume, measured in kilograms per cubic meter (kg/m³).
steps: Mass kg divided by volume m³
questions.fastStrategy: Density unit = kg/m³.

questions.question: If area at a pipe's outlet is half the inlet area (steady incompressible flow), the outlet speed is:
questions.explanation: Continuity: A1v1 = A2v2. If A2 = 0.5 A1, then v2 = v1 × (A1/A2) = v1 × 2.
questions.fastStrategy: Half the area → double the speed (steady incompressible).

questions.question: Absolute pressure equals atmospheric pressure plus:
questions.explanation: Absolute pressure = gauge pressure + atmospheric pressure.
questions.fastStrategy: Absolute = gauge + atmospheric.
